sections.title: Nine vowels: copy the mouth first
body: Swedish has nine vowel letters: A, O, U, Y, I, E, Ö, Ä, Å. First copy the lip and tongue position; then copy the audio.
English, Hindi, and Marathi examples are memory bridges, not exact Swedish pronunciation. The Swedish recording is the final model.
Rounded lips: O, U, Y, Ö, Å. Front tongue: I, E, Y, Ä, Ö. Notice that Y and Ö belong to both groups.

examples.note: Open for A; round for O.
Keep the lips rounded; move the tongue forward for Y.

examples.en: I, E, Ö, Ä, and Å lesson words

features.label: Rounded lips
features.note: O, U, Y, Ö and Å push the lips forward into a circle. Check in a mirror.

features.label: Front vowels
features.note: E, I, Y, Ä and Ö keep the tongue forward. Remember this group: it softens g, k and sk in topic 4.

sounds.cue: Open wide and let the sound sit at the back of the mouth. आ is a starting bridge.
Round the lips as in boots. In these words Swedish O sounds close to a long oo.
Tight rounded lips, as if drinking through a straw. Long u in du and short u in dum sound different: copy each one.
Say I, keep the tongue still, and round the lips as for U.
Wide smile, tongue high and forward. ई is a starting bridge.
A lighter smile than I. ए is a starting bridge.
Say E, keep the tongue still, and round the lips as for O.
Drop the jaw as for A, but aim for E. Near the e in bed.
The real O: deep and round. ऑ or English aw is a starting bridge.

sections.title: Long or short: stretch one part
body: In a stressed Swedish syllable, either the vowel is long or the consonant after it is long. Hear both parts, not only the vowel.

A common spelling clue is: one consonant letter after the stressed vowel often means a longer vowel; a doubled consonant often means a short vowel and longer consonant. It is a clue, not a rule without exceptions.
Use the routine: find the stressed vowel → look right → listen → copy the whole word.

examples.note: Stretch the a in tak; stop it quickly and hold the k in tack.
Hear the stressed final é in kafé and the short a plus long f in kaffe.
Bor has a long stressed vowel; the doubled consonants signal short stressed vowels in the other words.

rows: cut the vowel; hold the consonant

sections.memoryTip: Single often means STRETCH. Double often means STOP the vowel quickly—but always check the stressed syllable and listen.

activity.label: Stretch or stop?
activity.title: Predict the length from the spelling, then check by ear
activity.instructions: Look at the highlighted stressed vowel and the letters after it. Choose stretch or stop, then play the word to confirm.

buckets.label: Stretch
buckets.hint: long vowel · one consonant after it

buckets.label: Stop
buckets.hint: short vowel · two consonants after it

items.why: One k after the a: stretch the a.
ck counts as a double consonant: cut the a and hold the k.
One k after the o: stretch it.
Double f: a short a and a long f.
One r after the o: stretch it.
Double m: stop the a quickly and hold the m.
Nothing follows the stressed y, so it is long.
Double p: short a, long p.
One n after the å: stretch it.
Double t: short ö, long t.
Two different consonants, s and t, also usually mean a short vowel.
Double g after the stressed u: keep the u short.

activity.summary: One consonant after the stressed vowel usually means stretch. Two consonants usually mean stop. It is a strong clue, not a law, so the recording always has the final say.

sections.title: One vowel group, three soft sounds
body: The spelling group E, I, Y, Ä, Ö often softens the consonant immediately before it. These are front vowels because the tongue is forward; Y and Ö still use rounded lips.
G usually becomes the Swedish j sound, K usually becomes the tj sound /ɕ/, and SK usually becomes the sj sound /ɧ/ before this group.
TJ is not exactly English ch, and SJ is not exactly English sh. Use the shortcut to predict, then use audio to learn the actual sound. Some loanwords are exceptions.

examples.note: The first vowel is Ä or I.
Swedes call it the tjugo sound (tjugo = 20): a small, sharp hiss with the tongue forward. Do not add an English t + ch.
The sju sound (sju = 7): deeper and further back than tj. It varies by region and speaker.

examples.en: hard sk before A and U
examples.note: No front vowel follows sk.
One short sentence for repeated K + front-vowel practice.

k + e, i, y, ä, ö

sections.memoryTip: Same five soft vowels, three different results: G → J, K → TJ, SK → SJ. Tjugo (20) is the small, sharp sound; sju (7) is the big, deep one. Do not call them both ‘sh’.

activity.label: Sound detective
activity.title: Look at the letter after g, k, or sk, then predict the sound
activity.instructions: Swedish teachers call e, i, y, ä, ö the soft vowels (mjuka vokaler) and a, o, u, å the hard vowels (hårda vokaler). Soft vowel next? The consonant usually softens too. Hard vowel next? It stays hard. Choose, then listen.

buckets.hint: as in ja · g + soft vowel

buckets.label: tj sound
buckets.hint: as in tjugo · k + soft vowel, or tj

buckets.label: sj sound
buckets.hint: as in sju · sk + soft vowel, sj, skj

buckets.label: No change
buckets.hint: a hard vowel (a, o, u, å) follows

items.why: G + ä, a front vowel: it starts like Swedish j.
K + i, a front vowel: the soft tj sound.
A is a back vowel, so sk stays hard: s + k.
Sk + ä, a front vowel: the sj sound.
G + i: the Swedish j sound.
A is a back vowel, so k stays hard.
K + ö: Ö is rounded but still a front vowel, so k softens.
Sj is always the sj sound, whatever vowel follows.
U is a back vowel, so sk stays hard.
K + ö, a front vowel: the tj sound.
Skj is always the sj sound, even before o.
G + i: the Swedish j sound.
Tj is always the tj sound.
Sk + i: the sj sound, as in Solen skiner.

activity.summary: One question does most of the work: which vowel comes next? Front vowels (e, i, y, ä, ö) soften g, k and sk into three different sounds; back vowels leave them hard. Sj, skj and tj keep their sound whatever follows. Some loanwords break the rule, so trust the recording.

sections.title: Recognise the remaining Lesson 1 spellings
body: Recognition only today: SJ and SKJ normally use the sj sound, as in sjuk and skjorta. Initial HJ and LJ normally begin with the Swedish j sound, as in hjälp and ljus.
Dialect matters in Finland: Sweden-Swedish often merges RS in kurs into a retroflex sound, while Finland-Swedish usually keeps R + S. Many Finland-Swedish speakers also keep a clear D in djur.
Och is /ɔk/ in careful speech and is often shorter in conversation. Skönt normally means pleasant or comfortable; say fint hår or snyggt hår for a natural compliment.

examples.note: Two spellings for the sj sound.
Initial H or L is silent in these spellings; begin with Swedish j.
You may hear j alone in Sweden or a retained d in Finland-Swedish.
Keep r + s separate for a Finland-Swedish target.

sections.title: How are you? Pick an honest answer
body: Two everyday ways to ask: Hur är det? (How's it going?) and Hur mår du? (How are you feeling?). Both are friendly and fine with anyone.
Answer with the verb you hear: Hur är det? → Det är bra. Hur mår du? → Jag mår bra. You will also hear Jag är bra in casual speech.
Then send the question back with Och du?, the same move you learned in Lesson 1.

examples.fi: Hur är det? — Det är bra, tack.
examples.en: How's it going? — It's good, thanks.
examples.note: är det → det är: the answer mirrors the question.

examples.fi: Hur mår du? — Jag mår toppen!
examples.en: How are you? — I feel great!
examples.note: Toppen means great, top.

examples.fi: Så där. Jag är lite trött.
examples.note: Lite from Lesson 1 makes it softer.
Ganska means pretty, rather.
Inte (not) comes right after mår.

rows: Jag mår bra. · Det är bra.
Jag är trött. · Jag mår inte så bra.
I'm tired. · I don't feel so good.
Jag mår dåligt. · Jag mår ganska dåligt.
I feel bad. · I feel pretty bad.

sections.memoryTip: Mirror the question: är det → det är; mår du → jag mår. Then bounce it back: Och du?
sections.tryIt: Answer Hur mår du? three times: once how you really feel today, once great, once tired. End every answer with Och du?

activity.label: Mood meter
activity.title: Where does each answer sit on the mood meter?
activity.instructions: Read or hear each answer and place it on the meter. There is no wrong mood, only the right words for it.

items.why: Toppen is the top of the meter.
Bra means good or fine.
The answer to Hur är det? Same mood as Jag mår bra.
Så där is the middle: not good, not bad.
Okej is okay, the middle of the meter.
Trött means tired: lower on the meter.
Dåligt means bad.
Jag mår + toppen: great.
Inte så bra: not so good.
Ganska dåligt: pretty bad.

activity.summary: Pick the answer that is true, then ask back with Och du? Honest answers make better conversations than always saying bra.

sections.title: Pronouns: point to people without names
body: Swedish subject pronouns: jag (I), du (you, one person), han (he), hon (she), hen (they, one person), vi (we), ni (you, two or more), de (they).
Count the people for you: du is one person, ni is two or more. Modern Swedish uses du with almost everyone, including teachers and shop staff.
Hen is one word for a person without saying he or she, just like Finnish hän. De is written de but said dom.

examples.fi: Det är Priya. Hon är min syster.
examples.en: That's Priya. She is my sister.
examples.note: Hon points back to Priya.

examples.fi: Det är Rohan. Han bor i Indien.
examples.en: That's Rohan. He lives in India.
examples.note: Han points back to Rohan.

examples.fi: Kim är min vän. Hen talar svenska.
examples.en: Kim is my friend. They speak Swedish.
examples.note: Hen: one person, no he or she.

examples.fi: Hej Alex och Elin! Hur mår ni?
examples.en: Hi Alex and Elin! How are you (both)?
examples.note: Two people, so ni.

examples.fi: Priya och Rohan? De bor i Indien.
examples.en: Priya and Rohan? They live in India.
examples.note: Write de, say dom.

sections.memoryTip: Ni is like Marathi तुम्ही: more than one person. Hen is like Finnish hän: one word for he or she.

activity.pattern: Jag, du, vi and ni include the speaker or the listener; han, hon, hen and de point to someone else. Du and ni both mean you, so count the people. Write de, say dom.

sections.title: People in your life: family and relationships
body: Build family sentences with Jag har … (I have) and Jag är … (I am): Jag har en syster. Jag är gift.
Swedish glues words together: pojke + vän = pojkvän (boyfriend), flicka + vän = flickvän (girlfriend). Bo means live, as in Jag bor i: a sambo lives together with a partner, a särbo lives apart.
Useful status words: gift (married), sambo, singel, skild (divorced), and Jag bor ensam (I live alone). Barn means child or children; syskon means brothers and sisters together.

examples.fi: Jag har en syster och en bror.
examples.en: I have a sister and a brother.
examples.note: En before one person: en syster, en bror.

examples.fi: Jag är sambo. Han heter Mikko.
examples.en: I live with my partner. His name is Mikko.
examples.note: Sambo: partners who live together without being married. Very common in Finland and Sweden.

examples.fi: Jag är gift. Jag har en fru.
examples.en: I'm married. I have a wife.
examples.note: Man = husband, fru = wife. Make and maka are formal words for spouse.

examples.fi: Jag är singel och jag bor ensam.
examples.en: I'm single and I live alone.
examples.note: Ensam = alone.

examples.fi: De har två barn, en son och en dotter.
examples.en: They have two children, a son and a daughter.
examples.note: Barn is both child and children.

rows: Jag är gift. Jag har en man.

sections.memoryTip: Bo = live. Jag bor i … (Lesson 1) → sambo (live together) → särbo (live apart). And a classic joke: gift means married, but ett gift is poison.
sections.tryIt: Say three true sentences about people in your life: one with Jag har …, one with Jag är …, and one with Hon heter … or Han heter …

activity.label: Build the word
activity.title: Glue the parts into one Swedish word
activity.instructions: Swedish builds new words by joining old ones. Match each pair of parts to the word it makes.

pairs.note: a joke word: an adult who still lives with their parents

activity.pattern: Knowing just vän (friend) and bo (live) unlocks five relationship words. Notice that pojke and flicka lose their last letter when they join vän.

sections.title: Question words: ask the next question
body: Vad = what, hur = how, var = where, varifrån = where from, när = when, varför = why, vem = who.
Word order: question word → verb → person. Var bor du? När kommer de? The verb always comes second.
A yes/no question starts with the verb itself: Är du gift? Har du syskon? Talar du svenska? Vilken, vilket and vilka (which) come in a later lesson.

examples.note: Vad asks for a thing.
Hur + a describing word: hur gammal.
Var asks for a place.
När asks for a time.
Varför asks for a reason. Ni: more than one person.
Vem asks for a person.

sections.memoryTip: Var and vad differ by one letter: var asks for a place, vad for a thing. Varför hides för: for what reason?
sections.tryIt: Ask yourself five questions aloud, each with a different question word, and keep the verb second: Var bor du? När kommer du? Varför pluggar du svenska?

activity.label: Answer detective
activity.title: Which question word does this answer belong to?
activity.instructions: Each card is an answer. Work backwards: is it a thing, a manner, a place, an origin, a time, a reason, or a person?

items.why: It answers Vad heter du? A name is a thing you ask for with vad.
It answers Hur mår du?
A place: Var bor du? — I Helsingfors.
Från signals an origin: Varifrån kommer du?
A time: När kommer de? — Nästa vecka.
A person: Vem är hon?

items.fi: För att jag bor i Finland.
items.why: För att (because) gives a reason: Varför pluggar du svenska?
It answers Hur smakar vegansk mjölk? from page 6.
A thing: Vad gillar du?

activity.summary: Every answer fits one question word. When you can hear which question an answer belongs to, you can also ask the next question yourself: question word, then verb, then person.

sections.title: Hear it the way people say it
body: Written and spoken Swedish differ a little. Recognise these short forms now, and keep writing the full forms.
De is said dom. Jag is often just ja. Är often shrinks to e, det to de, and vad to va.
So Hur är det? often sounds like hur e de?, and De mår bra sounds like dom mår bra.

examples.note: Heard as: dom bor i Indien.
Often heard as: ja mår bra.
Often heard as: hur e de?
Often heard as: va heter du?

sections.memoryTip: Write it full, hear it short. When fast Swedish sounds strange, try the full form in your head.
sections.tryIt: Play each example at normal speed, then slowly. Listen for dom, ja, e and va.

activity.label: Written → spoken
activity.title: Match each written word to how it often sounds
activity.instructions: On the left is what you write. On the right is what you often hear in everyday speech.
activity.pattern: Spoken Swedish drops or shortens small, frequent words. Write de, jag, är, det and vad in full; expect dom, ja, e, de and va when people talk fast.

assignment.title: Episode 2 mission: People in my life
assignment.instructions:
CORE: Answer Hur mår du? honestly and send it back with Och du? Then present two people in your life: who they are (Det är min …), their name (Hon heter … / Han heter …), and where they live.

QUESTION LOOP: Ask three questions with different question words, for example Var bor du? När kommer du? Varför pluggar du svenska? Keep the verb second.

RETURN: Without looking, say how you are and introduce one person in under 20 seconds.
assignment.model:

Det är min syster. Hon heter Priya. Hon bor i Indien.
Det är min vän. Hon heter Elin. Hon är sambo och hon bor i Helsingfors.
Var bor du? När kommer du? Varför pluggar du svenska?

takeaways: Mirror the question: Hur är det? → Det är bra. Hur mår du? → Jag mår bra. Then ask back: Och du?
Pronouns: jag, du, han, hon, hen, vi, ni, de. Count the people for du and ni; write de but say dom.
